column1: In January twenty twenty-five, India found out how fast that door can close.
Just days before leaving office, America's government put out a new rule.
It sorted the world into three groups.
Its closest allies could buy these chips freely.
China was blocked.
And India?
India was put in the middle group, with a limit on how many of these chips it could get.
Four months later, the new American government scrapped that rule.
But India had seen it.
The tap is in someone else's hand.
So what would you do?
India didn't wait to own a giant reading room.
It rented one... and shared it.
Under the IndiaAI Mission, private companies put their chips into one common pool.
Indian startups and researchers rent time on them, and the government pays part of the bill.
In January twenty twenty-five, India lined up more than eighteen thousand chips for that pool.
By June twenty twenty-six, more than forty-five thousand.
That's a big jump, right?
But by the end of twenty twenty-four, one American company, Meta, said it would have around three hundred and fifty thousand of these chips.
Almost eight times your country's whole shared pool this June.
And the money?
India's whole A.I. mission is about ten thousand crore rupees, spread over five years.
This year alone, Meta told its investors it would spend around thirteen lakh crore rupees on buildings and machines, much of it for A.I.
